speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I desire to lay on the Table a return to an Order of the House dated 3rd April, 1922, for a copy of all correspondence passed during the year 1921 between the Prime Minister of Canada and the Prime Minister of Ontario relating to the activities of Hon. Manning Doherty in England on the subject of the cattle embargo. My right hon. friend yesterday made special mention of this report. I think it is perhaps due to him that I should give the explanation as to .why the return was not brought down immediately. I will therefore read a memorandum which has been handed to me by the Under Secretary of State for External Affairs:
I send herewith the return ordered by the House of Commons on the motion of Mr. White for correspondence relating to the activities of the Hon. Manning Doherty in England. There is no correspondence on this subject in this

department other than that contained in certain papers which the private secretary of the late Prime Minister left here about the time of the change of Government. I was not sure whether these papers were sent here for safekeeping, or to be accounted official and placed on the files of the department. I wrote two letters to the late Prime Minister's secretary asking this question, to neither of which I hav6 received any answer beyond a verbal message, whereas I asked for a written reply. Inasmuch, however, as Mr. Meighen is now pressing for these papers I assume there is no objection, in so far as he is concerned, to bringing them down. The papers have been ready since the 13 th April.

SUPPLY-DEFENCE FORCES *
On the motion of Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King (Prime Minister) for Committee of Supply:	_

Before
the House goes into Supply, I would like to address a few remarks on the work of the Militia of Canada, and of preparedness on the part of this country. Many arguments have been advanced in this House as to shew why this country should dispense with defence forces, and it is my intention to deal with a few of these arguments, and to attempt to give this House some information which I have been privileged to gain by having seen certain things, so that we may be in a better position to deal with questions relating to the military forces of Canada when they come before us. The main arguments advanced against this country maintaining defence forces are: First, that there is no one proposing to attack us; second, that we have plenty of men trained now; third, that the people are sick of war; and, fourth, that disputes in
the future will be settled by conference rather than by arms.
With regard to the first question viz.: who is about to attack us, I would remind hon. members of the pre-war assurances which were given by the Prime Minister of England to the House of Commons of England and to the people of the British Empire, that war with Germany was not only not impending, but was out of the question. I would also remind hon. members of the futility of making prophecies about war, and would recall the examples we have before us of the past hundred years- the example of war with United States in 1812; our own civil wars, the American civil war; and the fact that we are to-day faced with greater armies than the world has ever before been faced with-armies which are to-day mobilized by Russia, France and many other countries.
As to the second argument which has been advanced-that we have plenty of trained men now: The only inference, Mr. Speaker, that one can gather from that argument is that those advancing it propose that those men who took part in the late war should be called upon again to defend the country should there be a war. I was particularly struck by a question which the hon. member from East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) put to the hon. gentleman for North Ontario (Mr. Halbert), the other evening when he asked whether it was the intention of that member that these men should again be called upon. The reply was "I had as many friends in kahki as the hon. gentleman who asked the question had I do not think that many hon. members wish to take credit to themselves for what their friends did in the late war, but there has been altogether too much talk about the number of trained men that we have to-day. We have many trained men, it is true; but they will be useful in this country only in teaching the coming generation the lessons gathered during the late war. I do not expect that *here will be war in our time, or war, at any rate, that these men will be called upon to take part in; but they should be f ailed upon now to complete the duty that they attempted to perform overseas, by passing on the lessons which they learned.
Then, there is the third argument-that the people are sick of war. The people who are really sick of war to-day are the people who served, the people who gave their sons, who gave their all during the war; but the people who talk most to-day
Defence Forces

about being sick of war are those Who are sick of their shame at not having done their duty in the past. Let me read the remarks of General William T. Sherman in this connection:
I confess without shame that I am tired and sick of war. Its glory is all moonshine. Even success, the most brilliant, is over dead and mangled bodies, the anguish and lamentations of distant families, appealing to me for missing sons, husbands and fathers. It is only those who have not heard a shot, nor the shrieks and groans of the wounded, friend or foe, who cry aloud for more blood, more vengeance, more desolation.
It is safe to say that those sentiments are the sentiments of every soldier; but despite those sentiments, I feel convinced that the great body of returned soldiers are still prepared to sacrifice themselves, should the honour of this country require them to do so in the future.
Then, we hear this .argument advanced: We look forward to the day when disputes will be settled by conference and not by arms. I agree, and I think all hon. members will agree, that we look forward to that day; but statesmen of all ages have recognized that the way to prevent war is to be reasonably prepared for war. What, for instance, would be the position of Mr. Lloyd George in the conferences which are taking place in Europe to-day if he were not backed by the force which is represented by the .British army and navy? Would any one suggest that he would be listened to if he had demobilized the British army and navy? Had he done so, no respect whatever would be paid to the remarks or arguments which might be advanced by him in those conferences. We have Sir Henry Wilson's classification, based upon that principle recognized by statesmen, of armies into three classes: First, those armies which are strong enough to prevent war; second, those armies which are too weak to prevent war, but which are strong enough to win war; and third, those armies which can only lose a war. Into which class does Canada fall? Canada has no army; Canada does not fall into any of these categories. But hon. members will say: What about Canada's part in the late war? True, Canada did magnificently in the late war; but it was fully three years after the war had commenced that Canada was prepared for war; that she was prepared to strike as an independent country should be if it is going to be able to stand as an independent nation, and apparently hon. members desire that Canada should stand as an independent nation.

I should like to bring to the attention of the House a comparison between the achievements of the forces of Canada and the forces of that great republic to the south of us during the last hundred days of the war, for the purpose, not of reflecting upon that great republic, but of showing what can be accomplished by a country with a trained army and what is accomplished by a country which is not fully prepared. The United States, unfortunately for them, were three years behind Canada in entering the war, and the result was that they were not able to make the showing per capita that the Canadians were able to make. I should like to give a few figures of the numbers engaged, the casualties, and the success achieved during that period. For instance, during that time the Americans bad 650,000 troops engaged; the Canadians, 105,000. The Americans were engaged during 47 days of operations; the Canadians, 100 days. The battle casualties of the Americans were 100,000; of the Canadians, 45,830. The prisoners taken by the Americans were 16,000; by the Canadians, 31,537. Guns captured by the Americans numbered 468; by the Canadians, 623. Machine guns captured by the Americans numbered 2,864; by the Canadians, 2,842. Trench mortars captured by the Americans numbered 177; by the Canadians, 336. Territory freed by the Americans covered 610 square miles; by the Canadians, 336 square miles. Villages freed by the Americans numbered 150; by the Canadians, 228. German divisions met and defeated by the Americans numbered 46; by the Canadians, 47. Casualties per German division /defeated by the Americans numbered 2,170; by the Canadians, 975. The maximum advance by the Americans was 34 miles; by the Canadians, 86 miles. These favourable results were made possible only by the fact that the Canadians had benefited by the experience of training and hard fighting during the previous years. My point is this: Is there any one here who will take the responsibility of denying the youth of our country an opportunity of learning the lessons learned by the men who took part in that war? Is there any one who would take the responsibility of unnecessarily exposing the youth of succeeding generations to useless slaughter when by taking full advantage of the lessons learned we could prepare them to take their part in any operations which may become necessary in the future?

Defence Forces
We hear much talk about Canada being an independent nation. The Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) the other evening asked whether we were going to go back one hundred and fifty years and become Crown colonists to be looked after by Great Britain and not by ourselves. We hear a great deal of talk about Canada's responsibility as a nation. We hear it vehemently stated that we are an independent nation, independent of Great Britain and of all other countries. I suggest that we should not deceive ourselves. We have no army in this country; we have no forces which can be counted upon even to defend ourselves. We are sponging to-day, as we have in the past, upon the Mother Country, both for defence and for possible offence. We are absolutely dependent upon Great Britain for our protection both on land and sea.
We in this country are not preparing for war. The proposal has never been made by the Minister of Militia or by any member of this House that we should prepare for war. If we were to prepare for war it would require for a period of years a vote of at least fifteen times the amount which it is proposed to make for annual training. We could not actively prepare for war on a vote of less than $150,000,000 per annum over a period of years. That was conclusively proven during the late war by the operations in which the Canadians took part. The ex-service men in this country resent the suggestion that by training and passing on these lessons we are preparing for war. They resent still further making a political football of the issue of national defence in Canada. We have had in cnis House the sorry spectacle of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) opposing in the past estimates for the purposes of the militia, and this year bringing down similar estimates as a part of Government policy. We have heard him protesting against Canada having a reserve of ammunition for her guns, Attempts have been made during the past six months to make political capital out of the bringing into this country of a few shells which already belonged to Canada, and which would have been wasted if we had not taken them. Those shells, Mr. Speaker, which we have wasted so much time in talking about, could be fired in one hour by the artillery of Canada to-day. Yet the Prime Minister has spent twenty or thirty hours in talking about those shells. With regard to their cost, even if we had been called on to pay for them, the
amount required would not exceed the amount which was required to supply our guns for one day during the last hundred days of the war. I venture to say that the forces which are lining themselves up today to oppose training consist of those who are uninformed, and in that class I have no hesitation in placing the Prime Minister himself. Secondly, I would include those who would profit by disruption in this country and by the disintegration of constitutional government in Canada.
It has been suggested that a break in the training of our militia for a period of one year or more would do no harm.

Mr. Speaker, I submit that the hon. member is not in order in discussing on a motion to go into Committee of Supply the question of annual training, which has already been referred to a Committee of the Whole House.

I do not propose to discuss the question of annual training. I think the hon. member is mistaken. Possibly I did refer to annual training, but I intended to refer to it only in its broad aspect and in connection with the militia as a whole.

I think every one is
familiar with the old rule of the House of Commons, that a motion to go into Supply is the occasion for any hon. member to present his grievances. "No Supply without redress of grievances," is the old standing rule of British parliamentary government, and when a motion is made: That the Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Supply,-any member can rise and discuss any grievances which he may have. I will read to the House the comments made on this point by Bouri-not, based, I may say, on May, the highest authority on parliamentary procedure:
The order of the day for the House to go into committee of supply having been read, the Speaker will put the question "That I do now leave the chair."
That is the question now before the House. He goes on:
The same question is always put whenever the house is to go into committee of supply, in order to afford an opportunity to members to propose amendments. On this point it is observed by an eminent authority that the ancient constitutional doctrine that the redress of grievances is to be considered before the granting of supplies, is now represented by the practice of permitting every description of amendment to be moved on the question for the Speaker leaving the chair, before going into committee of supply or ways and means.

Defence Forces

Further on he says:
The ordinary rules of dehate are applicable on this occasion; for instance, a matter already decided by the House, or of which notice has been given, or which stands upon the orders of the day, cannot be discussed; nor can any subject or matter of detail which should be discussed in committee, be debated on these occasions ; nor can debate or amendment be permitted relating to grants already agreed to, or to resolutions which will be proposed in the committee, or in the committee of ways and means, or to items in the estimates.
In the present instance I do not find the point of order is well taken, because the hon. member is speaking on the necessity of maintaining our militia on its present footing, and his remarks are of a general character. If he were speaking of the estimates of the Militia Department which were under discussion last week, he would be clearly out of order; but so far I think he is in order, and such is my ruling.

I was dealing with the assertion that a break in the training will do no harm. I have no hesitation whatever in saying that such a break, even of one year, will do an irreparable injury to the militia. We have to-day a large class of returned officers and non-commissioned officers who, under great pressure, have been persuaded to stay with the militia, to teach our youth the lessons learned and so pass on to them their own first-hand knowledge acquired at the front. Many of these officers and non-commissioned officers have already quit the militia in utter disgust because they are not receiving that encouragement which they might reasonably expect to receive; and although others are remaining, they are becoming discouraged by the apathy with which they are faced. Those men feel that while they performed a certain duty in fighting for their country, there is still the all-important duty for them to perform of passing on the knowledge gained at the front. That is why they are prepared to remain with the militia at their own expense and at great personal sacrifice.
There is also this danger, that should a man drop out of active training for even a short time, he rapidly loses touch and would soon be classed among those soldiers who in the late war were known as "dug-outs". I do not use that term disparagingly, because it applied to a very large class of retired ex-officers who promptly came forward at the outbreak of war and gave their services to their country. But if our men do not continue their training they soon get out of touch with the latest
fMr. Speaker.]
methods of offence and defence and their usefulness is to that extent impaired.
I need not enlarge upon the patriotic effect that a little training will have upon our youth, or upon the improvement in their physical well-being. I think we can compare the individual with the nation, because after all our nation is only a combination of individuals. We may very well take the example of the boy at school. How much prouder we are of a boy who is brought up to defend himself and to be proud of his physical well-being-of the boy who is not "too proud to fight," to use an expression we have heard a good deal in the last few years.
The proposals which had been before this House in the past are merely to enable us to maintain and train a nucleus of instructors so that if we are called upon to take our part in any future war we will have the few men necessary to instruct the large body of recruits that will constitute our army. The fact that this country is spending less per capita on its military training than any other country in the world, including all the British Dominions, is surely proof that we are not preparing for war. Certainly there is no class in this country less imbued with the idea that we should prepare for war than that class which at present compose our militia and ex-service men generally throughout the country.
How are our militia units maintained? It is generally supposed, I imagine, that our officers, non-commissioned officers and men are being paid by the country for their militia services. In the past they have received, it is true, a small grant for their training, but the money which has been granted has been returned to the units so that they may efficiently "carry on" with their training. The farmers of this country have benefited by that grant, because from it are purchased the supplies used in the military camps.
Now, Mr. Speaker, before I close these remarks-*
Hear, hear.

I know it is distasteful
to some hon. members to hear our national defence discussed. I know also that there are many members here who probably disapprove of Canada's participation in the late war. But I felt it my duty to give hon. members-at least, those on the Liberal side-an opportunity of considering this matter, because I understand that a caucus will be held tomorrow when they will decide

Defence Forces
whether they are going to scrap the militia or not, and before they do so I thought I should at least place the matter before them as squarely as I could, even although they do not appear to be prepared to listen to my arguments. At any rate, I feel that I have done my part. But I should like to congratulate the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) upon the manly stand he took on this subject when the estimates of his department were being discussed. I should like also to express my sympathy with the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and other members of his party who do not see the benefits and advantages of a limited defence force, because I quite appreciate that they have been taught in the past, and have apparently grown to believe, that in principle any expenditure on the militia is wrong. Their own leader sought to teach them that. Therefore is it any wonder that to-day, even though their own party now brings down as Government policy certain estimates, those hon. members are not convinced by such a sudden change of front, and bring forward the amendments that were proposed last week? I would like to see the Liberal party consider this question from the point of view of the national honour of this country. It is a national question; and I hope that if they do meet in caucus before the estimates again come up for discussion, they will seriously reflect before accepting any compromise proposed by men so ill-informed on the subject as the member who moved the amendment to the item which we were discussing the other evening. I believe that the militia estimates which the Government have brought down have been pared to the bone; and if any criticism can be offered in regard to the manner in which the Government has dealt with them, it is that they have been too niggardly rather than too extravagant in their proposals.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Militia and Defence): Mr. Speaker, I will not discuss questions which will more appropriately be dealt with in Committee of the Whole. But I want to say in defence of the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), that he won distinction in the war, he won the right to take any position he likes on this question. And I have every respect for his opinion. So far from being misinformed, he is a man who is fully informed. We may disagree on details, but I want to point out that the member for Quebec South is in a position, through years of service on his own part and on the
85i
part of other members of his family, to speak on military matters.
As to the caucus, I am afraid my hon. friend (Mr. Clark) cannot get in, and if he did, he might not stay long. However, the Liberal party, notwithstanding anything that has been said on the estimates is here as a unit to do what it thinks is in the interests of this country, and it will emerge from all the criticism with credit to itself and to the men in it, no matter what their individual views may be. I do not want to say a cross word to my hon. friend, but if he wants to go back to the time when people were taking peculiar positions,
I would refer him to the year 1911, when he was standing side by side with the men who did not want to do anything for the British Empire.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it will be observed that there is a reduction of $505,000 as compared with the amount appropriated last year. On page 24 of the Estimates it will be noted that last year $625,000 was voted for salaries and contingent expenses of the Board of Pension Commissioners. During the year the activities of the Board of Pension Commissioners were, to a very large degree, merged with those of the 'Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-estaplish-ment, and this year for the same
4 p.m. service only $71,000 is asked for, being a reduction of $554,000. Adding to this the $505,000, therefore, the reduction in appropriation for salaries this year is over $1,000,000.
How much of the $625,000 was spent last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: In round figures, $500,000. After careful consideration of the whole matter and consultation with the officials of the department, we have come to the conclusion that a further reduction may be effected so far as provision for salaries is concerned. Therefore, I would move, that the item of salaries be reduced by $195,000. It is the opinion of the officials, and of myself, after surveying the field, that we will be able to meet all our obligations even after this reduction is made.

I commend my hon. friend for cutting down all the expenses

Supply-Re-Establishment
that he can, but I would ask him if the reduction is not entirely due to the fact that the work of the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment is lessening owing to the condition which prevails-that is that most, or a great many, of the men have been attended to medically, and from a vocational standpoint, and that there has been lessening in other branches of the work? I would like to have my hon. friend's opinion upon that point. *

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My hon. friend is partly right in that there is a great contraction in the activities of the department. That applies especially to the vocational training. My hon. friend was not in the House the other day when this question was under consideration, otherwise he would have heard the statement I made as to the reduction in the number of men who are actually being trained. I think the reduction is from some four or five thousand last year to six hundred this year. A great reduction in the expenditure has also been effected through the amalgamation of the staff of the Board of Pension Commissioners with the staff of the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment.

When was that
effected?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It was effected during the course of last year. The staff, I think, was merged in the month of July.

I would like to ask my hon. friend another question. He said the cutting down of the expenditure was partly due to the natural reduction of the staff owing to the work being completed. I thought it was wholly due to that fact. If not would my hon. friend explain to the committee what the other part of the reduction, in addition to the natural reduction because of the lessening of the work, is due to?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I explained to my hon. friend that there was a reduction due to the fact that some of the activities of the department were lessened, also that a reduction was effected owing to the amalgamation of two important staffs.

I quite understand, but the point I was trying to make was exactly what the minister has pointed out-that the reduction is due to the natural lessening of the work that is going on in the department. What I wanted to make clear was that there was no real cutting down in these expenditures due to any special

economies. The reason I want to make that point clear is, not in order to establish that my hon. friend has not made any special reductions, but because I do not believe this is a department that can par

ticularly stand reductions, except where the lessening of the work permits of that being done.
I presume the cost per capita will be greater now than it formerly was on account of fewer men being taken care of?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am informed that the cost has not materially increased-
Not materially increased?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: -and that high salaried officials are being let out, although not in as large number as the lower salaried officials.
I presume they were let out last year, too?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No doubt there was a reduction last year.

Does not the minister think the time is approaching when it would be safe and proper to amalgamate the department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment with some of the other departments of government-perhaps in somewhat the same manner as was done in the case of the departments of naval service and militia? When the department was created during the war, it was understood by everybody that it was a department for purely war purposes and would not continue indefinitely. The work at the time of the creation of the department was enormous, but I suppose that in 1917,	1918 and 1919 that work
had reached the peak. I do not know what the estimates for those years were but I observe that the amount for the year 192021 was $40,000,000. For 1921-22 it had come down to $19,307,000; and for this year the estimate has again come down to $15,148,000. From these figures one can see that the work of the department is contracting, and rapidly contracting, each year. Now, will the minister consider the question of wiping out the department, or, at all events, amalgamating it with some other department of government? The time cannot be far distant when the work of this department will be finished, just as the work of the Soldier Settlement Board will be finished. The work of the Pension Commission, I suppose, will go on for many

Supply-R e-Esta blishment
years to come; but the number under vocational training has gone do>wn from 4,000 last year to, in round numbers, 600 this year. Next year I would think that work would be completed. Perhaps the minister could give the committee some information as to what, in his opinion, would be the approximate time when this department might cease to exist? It is an extra department of the Government and was only created for the purposes of the war. Some day the purposes of the department will be finished. As the expenditure this year is doiwn to $15,000,000 I would chink the time is not very far distant.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I cannot state even approximately when the Department of Soldiers' -Civil Re-establishment should disappear in some other branch of the ministry. Undoubtedly that day will come; the activities of the department have decreased in a large measure. But my hon. friend will note that those activities have decreased mainly in those branches of the work for which a certain period had been set after which no applications could be received-as for example in the case of vocational training. In that case, 1st February, 1920, was the date fixed after which	no application could be received, unless it was from a man who had been on the strength of the department in one of our institutions. As far as the patients are concerned, it is almost impossible to give anything like an exact idea as to when this activity will come to an end. The number of patients now being treated by the department is almost as large as it was a year ago, there is a difference only of about 400 out of 5,000 to 6,000, and the probability is that the decrease in the number of patients on our hands in the future will be very small indeed. A number are developing into chronic cases. Eventually the country will have to provide for them in some institutions other than regular hospitals. Among those chronic cases I might mention the mental cases, which ultimately will have to be dealt with perhaps in a different manner from the way they are being dealt with at the present time. Personally I would have no objection to merging this department in some other department, but I do not believe the time has yet come, in the interests of the returned men, to adopt such a course.

I am much obliged for the information. I quite see that, in regard to the mental cases, and the hospital cases,
the work that is being performed by the department will have to continue for a number of years. But that does not necessarily involve the maintenance of the department; the work could be carried on in connection with some other department. I assume that, perhaps, the majority of the cases in the hospital at the present time are in the nature of chronic cases. It will be the duty of Canada to look after these patients, probably, throughout their lives, and some department of the Government will have to function in the matter, and that applies to the majority of the mental cases. But it must be remembered that the Department of Militia has a hospital system of its own and is accustomed to looking after military patients, and I think it is worth while considering whether we are not now approaching the time when all the work done by this department might be handed over to the Department of Militia and carried on there without the additional expense of maintaining two departments. I will refer to the items in the present estimates on page 59. I do not know what the first item "Capital, $75,000" refers to. The second item, "Care of patients and medical examination of pensioners $4,000,000," will probably have to continue for some time, but it can be administered by another department with a great saving of expense. The next item, "Vocational expense," is decreasing to such an extent that next year, I should imagine, it will be wiped out altogether. The next item, "Salaries," I am glad to know, is coming down. I assume that that includes salaries in connection with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment hospitals that must come down very rapidly for a great many years yet to come. Then we have the item "Pay and allowances $3,500,000"; that is pay and allowances of the men who are actually in the hospitals according to their ranks. That could all be done by the Militia Department quite as conveniently as by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, with a single expenditure where a double expenditure is involved at the present time, with both departments paying these salaries. Then we have "Vocational loans $75,000." I assume that will vanish by next session. We have "Interest on war service gratuity," a very small item, which, I imagine, will vanish. Then, "Unemployment relief," is not in the nature of a fixed charge; on that score something may have to be granted for some years to come, but another department could handle that with a saving in expense. The next

Supply-R e-Esta blishment
item is "Operating expenses and working capital $700,000." I am not sure to what that item applies, but I notice there is a substantial reduction in it. It is more than cut in two, showing that it is rapidly diminishing, and will some day, I hope, reach the vanishing point. In the whole list there is no work, I submit, which could not be performed by the Militia Department, which has hospitals accustomed to the care of patients. Their pay staff is organized for the purpose, the main items could all be taken care of, and the department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, which was only temporarily adopted in this country, would soon come to the vanishing point and a large overhead would be saved to the country. I know the minister is quite reasonable in his view of the matter and will not prolong the existence of the department a day more than is necessary. I would like to impress upon him the desirability of bringing it to an end as soon as possible, because the whole department as now constituted can, I believe, be well administered by another department and the expense of one department be saved to the country.

(Kingston) : I wish to say a few words in regard to the salaries. I will only refer to one branch. I would like to ask the minister if the department has given any consideration to the establishment of soldiers' homes for the care of indigent exservice men? I am satisfied the care of these men will have to be taken up sooner or later by this Parliament

sooner, I fear, than later-and it seems to me that not only should the matter engage the attention of this department, or some other department of the government, but that a definite policy should be laid down in respect to it-the treatment of these veterans should not be left to local charitable persons. I happen to know of a case in my own county where a man is in a state of incurable illness. I regret to say that he is a returned soldier. He has been examined by medical boards, and they say his present disabilities were not the direct result of war services, consequently they have declined to take care of him and he is now being cared for by friends. Whether the official statement is well-founded, I cannot say, but the man went overseas and has no means of support- he will have to go into an almshouse or some other institution, and I regret to say that in the province of New Brunswick there is no institution in which he can be placed. His case may be one of many, and it does seem to me that some policy should be adopted and something done to take care of cases of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Of the vote of $100,000 a very small amount was spent, because the provisions came into existence only in January of this year. The number of pensions issued monthly in respect to disablement is 47,327; in respect to death, 19,490, a total of 66,817 pensioners in Canada. That does not include, of course, the dependents of either the disabled or the soldiers who have fallen. The last time
these estimates were before the House it was my privilege to explain that pensioners with a disability ranging between 5 and 14 per cent have the option of taking a lump sum or of receiving their pension monthly. A large number of pensioners have availed themselves of this provision and have decided to accept a final payment. The number of pensioners who have done so is 22,351 and the total amount paid in lump sums to these pensioners is $9,210,312. Besides that disabilities of a very minor nature, not over 5 per cent, are settled by the Board of Pension Commissioners regardless of the wishes of the men, and this amount is called a gratuity. Gratuities have been paid in lieu of pensions to 17,000 men, with a disability ranging between one inclusive and five exclusive, and the expenditure on this account has been $821,000. The total expenditure on pensions to date is $113,589,414.50. It will be noticed by the committee that an increase of $2,041,640,-appears in this appropriation. The amount which was voted last year was $30,958,359; but that amount did not meet the requirements of the year, because a large amount had to be paid for commutation,-the payment of the lump sum to which I have just referred,-and when the supplementary estimates for the year ended 31 March last are before the House an amount of $4,000,000 will have to be provided for that object. Therefore, in reality, there is not an increase in this item. The Board of Pension Commissioners who, as members of the committee know, are alone responsible for the awarding of pensions, expect that, with $33,000,000, they will be in a position to meet the obligations for pensions for the year just commenced.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The Board of Pension Commissioners is a tribunal and, in the short space of time that I have been at the head of the department, I have been unable to study very deeply the work of the board during the time it has been in operation. I have full confidence in Col. Thompson and the two other gentlemen who are associated with him; I think they are honest and impartial in their decisions. In the awarding of pensions they rely mainly upon the reports, mostly medical, which are submitted to them. The task is not an easy one; it is difficult. It may happen that, throughout the country, a certain number of pensioners receive pensions to which they are not entitled. On the other hand, it may happen that the number of men applying for pensions have been deprived of or refused such pensions or turned down when they should have been awarded pensions. The question is one of information on the part of the commissioners, and also one of appreciation on the part of the medical doctors who are in charge of the different examinations.

Medicine is not an exact science; doctors disagree in their appreciation of the same case. Some doctor may think the ailment of one particular ex-service man is to be traced to his war service, whilst another doctor will think it cannot be traced. The whole question of the awarding of pensions is summed up in this phrase-a pension is awarded to a disabled ex-service man when his disability can be attributed to his war service. The pension commissioners have to govern themselves by this principle. To say that I have not received any complaints would be not to state the facts correctly. I have certainly received a large number of complaints from men who thought they were entitled to receive a pension and who were refused the same. In reply to the remarks of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), I am not in a position to say if, in every case, justice has been done entirely; I am absolutely satisfied that the three commissioners have acted conscientiously in the discharge of their duties, but they are fallible like every human being.

I agree with practically everything the minister has said in regard to this matter. May I offer a suggestion regarding pensioners or those who think they should be pensioned? I believe my suggestion will probably meet with his approval, and I think it will meet with the approval of most hon. members. When men wish for another board, they should more easily obtain it than is, perhaps, the case at the present time. In other words a man, let us say, has had his pension discontinued or he has not received a pension when he thinks he should receive one, and he sometimes finds it rather difficult to obtain another board. That is, some medical board has passed upon his case and decided that he has no right to a pension, but the man is firmly convinced that he has a right to a pension. He may or may not be right; probably he is wrong, for I believe that when the board decides against the applicants, in the majority of cases the applicants are wrong. If there is any doubt on the question and certainly if there is doubt enough to enable the man to obtain from another doctor, perhaps a civilian, a letter to the effect that he thinks perhaps the man's conditon is due to war service-he should be able easily to obtain another medical board and have his case reviewed. I should like to impress on the minister what has been impressed on me many times in my capacity as a private

Supply-Re-Establishment
member of Parliament-I was not long enough minister to have it impressed upon me in that capacity-and as a medical man, and that is that these secondary boards, and boards later than secondary, should be obtained fairly easily when a man feels very strongly that he should receive a pension, or that his pension should not be cut down.

In putting the question I put a moment ago with regard to representation of the province of Quebec on the board, I want it to be understood that I did not want to detract in any way from the merits of the commissioners; but as this is a bilingual country and there is a large number of people dealing with the board of French origin and using the French language, I think we should keep up the time-honoured custom of giving representation on these important tribunals to the minority of the Canadian population. tions from the board because the duties were such that the commissioners entrusted with them felt the remuneration was not sufficient, and new ones were appointed. It is not always the easiest matter to get an appropriate man for a post of this sort. The feeling among the returned men is such that the appointee has virtually to be a returned man. Then he has to be a man with the experience-medical better than any other, except for the chairmanship- and also of some measure of business experience; and besides he must be willing to act. He must be a man of such standing as to command authority in his position. It is not always the easiest matter to get a man of that sort ready to take office. I remember, there was one-I shall not give his name, I do not think I should be asked to-who was pressed for appointment to this post. So far as political allegiance was concerned, everything that could be said was in his favour, but it was felt that the qualifications were not there. There was no other reason in the world why there was not a French Canadian appointee on this board. I agree with the hon. member for Bonaventure that if it can be done it is better, even though it is not essential as respects either English or French, that there should be representation of both races on important boards.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is moved by Mr. Neill that the first amendment be considered by the committee.

This amendment is the
same as the one I introduced a few nights ago-at least the effect of it will be the same. I am not bringing it forward in any spirit of obstruction. I simply believe that what transpired the other evening justifies me in again introducing this amendment to-night. Some hon. members who voted on the last occasion did not fully grasp the situation; others perhaps were absent. I feel, under the circumstances, that it is legitimate for me to introduce this amendment again. I will not waste the time of the committee by going over the arguments I used on the former occasion, but there are one or two points to which I wish to draw attention. If any hon. member will turn up Hansard and read the arguments in support of the bill passing without amendment advanced on that occasion, I believe he will be compelled to admit that there was very little solid reason given why my amendment should not pass. If hon. members will look at the speeches for and against the bill in its present form which were made the other night, they will find that there certainly was not a very strong argument advanced in favour of the measure. The amendment I ask is that the company shall begin operations within one year of the

passing of this legislation. You will observe, Mr. Chairman, that the bill as drafted does not bring this railway under the Railway Act of Canada as regards the commencement of construction. Under that act the commencement of construction involves spending fifteen per cent of the money authorized for the building of the road within a particular period. By a special clause in the present bill however, the company take themselves out of the operation of the Railway Act of Canada and therefore that section is not operative with respect to them. The effect of it is this: While they ask for two years in which to begin and five years in which to finish, the bill really gives them five years to begin, because " beginning " under the present bill means a most perfunctory operation. A few men with shovels could, in half a day, perform the perfunctory attempt at commencement which could be constructed as a commencement within the meaning of the bill. Consequently while the company ask for two years in which to begin, they are really asking for five years provided the line is completed within that time. I therefore ask that that illusive period be reduced to one year in which the company shall at least make a pretence of beginning operations. I wish to read a letter and it is only a short communication, that I have received in connection with this bill. It is one of a number of letters that I have received but I will not burden the House by reading them all. I shall just read this communication because it is a typical one:
At the last meeting of the local branch of the United Farmers of British Columbia I was authorized to write to you to ask you to use your influence in every possible way, in the coming session of Parliament, to prevent the Esquimau and Nanaimo Railway Company from getting the extension of time they are asking for. We feel very strongly here that the railway company ought to put this extension through for three reasons: Frst, it would provide a considerable amount of work for men and teams; Second, it would open up a considerable amount of country where there is much good land available for agriculture and which would be cultivated if transportation were provided at a reasonable rate; Third, if would cut down the cost of freight. At present it costs about 70 cents per hundred to haul freight from Victoria to Courtenay 145 miles, and it costs 20 cents per hundred to haul it from Courtenay to Merville by motor truck a distance of 8 miles. This disparity in cost presses very hard on the farmer. We firmly believe that this system of railway companies getting their charters extended from year to year is a most pernicious one. They ought either to build or relinquish the charter ; unless there

Esquimau-Nanaimo Ry.
is some really legitimate reason why the railway should not be built at the time.
Trusting you will give this your earnest consideration.
The communication is signed by the secretary of the association which I may mention is mostly composed of returned soldiers. I could read resolutions from boards of trade, and other organizations, but the letter I have cited is a typical illustration of the feeling in that district. It may be true, as alleged the other night, that if this railway is not built by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company it will not be built at all. That may or may not be true but at least we can give somebody else an opportunity. The other day when we western members were enjoying the hospitality of the city of Quebec-a hospitality that was given, I may say, with the grace and kindliness so characteristic of the French-Canadian people-we were shown, amongst other places the Montmorency falls, and it was a pretty sight. But I could not help thinking while we were gazing at it that the Campbell river falls along the route of this railway would produce five times the amount of electrical power. Whilst the latter falls are not so high as the Montmorency falls they have a far larger volume of water and if, as it is rumoured, there are negotiations pending for harnessing these falls, it would be a mere flea bite for that company-because they could incorporate with four or five millions-to build this jerk-water road to connect with the Canadian Pacific railway-It would pay them to build it to bring up supplies for this work. And whilst it is not an absolute fact at present we are not likely to obtain the building of the road by any other company while there is the assurance that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will have a blanket charter over it for all time. I have no hostility towards the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in this matter nor have the people whom I represent. I will say this, however: I will withdraw all opposition to this bill going through as it is framed if the hon. member in charge of the measure will postpone any further action upon it to-night and give me a written undertaking by that company that they will really build this railway within the time limits asked by themselves. That is all we ask.
If we had this assurance, and if there were anything like a reasonable probability or possibility that this road would be built, I would cheerfully concede the extra year to begin, and the extra year to finish

that road, but I am perfectly certain that that assurance will not be forthcoming. Can hon. members of this House believe that I should stand here and oppose a charter. of this kind, if there were any possibility of the road being built under it. What would my constituents think of such an act? Would I not be deluged, and would the House not be deluged, with telegrams and letters urging that I should consent to it? But the reason that these things are not forthcoming is that everything suggests that there is no probability of the line being built. I mentioned the other night the absence of the provision allowing for the issue of bonds for the road. That is an indication that they are not sincere in this matter to-night, and I think I can say without fear of contradiction that if this House passes this measure to-night, or this session-because it will not pass to-night-these people will be coming here two years hence asking for a further extension. It is not a revolutionary thing or an epoch-making thing. It is a simple amendment to give these people an opportunity to do what they declared on paper they wanted to do-to build this railway within a reasonable time.

It must be pointed out that this is only a reasonable request made by the railway company. It is quite a common thing for railway companies to do, particularly under the conditions which prevail now and have prevailed for a number of years. I do not think the railway company can be criticized for having delayed the building of the road, particularly when one is familiar with conditions in that part of Canada, and the difficulty in obtaining the material required for railway construction. This road goes through a section of country that is very rough, with very large trees, and in many cases it will require as high as one case to a case and a half of powder to blow out a single stump. It is only reasonable that the railway company should be given every opportunity to build this road at as reasonable a cost as possible. Many of the roads built in that section of British Columbia have not paid from the very beginning, on account of the tremendous outlay, the slow settlement, and the heavily timbered nature of the country. The primary reason for building the road, as I understand it, is to bring out the timber from that section of Vancouver island, and it is only after that timber is removed
Esquimalt-Nanaimo Ry.

and the land has been stumped, or partially stumped, that it will be ready for production, so that the delay in building the road will not be a very great inconvenience to the settlers in the very beginning. As to the Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway giving up this charter, and it being immediately taken up by some other railway company, I think that is very improbable indeed, because the Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway is the only railway in that section of Vancouver island, and if this road is to connect up and do any business, it must certainly connect up with the Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway at Courtenay. As far as giving a guarantee that this railway is going to be built is concerned, I am not in a position to do anything of the kind. I have not consulted the representatives of the railway with reference to this matter. This is a big company, well-known in Canada, doing business here, it has done a great deal to open up the West, and I think we can take its word just as well as we would that of any other business organization. Under these conditions, Mr. Chairman, I think the committee should not hesitate to grant the very reasonable request of the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway Company.

Much as I would like to agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), who has, in this House, spoken a good word for the province of Quebec, I am obliged to dissent from the opinion he expressed in reference to the extension of this charter, which I believe is being sought for very good reasons. The hon. gentleman has -stated that not many good reasons were advanced in favour of the bill a few weeks ago when the bill was before the House. But there are many good reasons, and some *of the members on this side of the House, \wh* were not present at the committee meeting, have not had time to go fully into the facts of the case concerning this application. I do not see the harm in extending for two years more a charter to a company which everybody knows is aided by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That railway company has built up this country and is one of the greatest railways in the world. We must consider also that there is no possibility, practically, of any other railway coming into competition with this railway or desiring to get a charter for the construction of this road. There is

also another factor. The hon. member for Comox has mentioned the possibility of immigrants, or other people from foreign lands, coming into this country, who might have to go away, because there were no possible facilities to enable them to go into the district of the Island of Vancouver which this railway is supposed to traverse. I might point out that I do not think there are very many immigrants coming from European countries who would go out very far on the Island of Vancouver, or even in the province of British Columbia. Most of these people settle in the central provinces of western Canada, and I think these people would suffer no great injury if a good company, like the one which has this charter at present, should have an extension granted for another two years. I do not hold in this House any brief, for the company which is asking for a renewal of its charter. When a company comes here supported by reliable people, and tells this bouse openly and frankly that, on accouni of certain conditions which have existed ir this country for the last two years, they have not been able to proceed with construction, an extension of a charter for twc years has never been refused. My hon. friend has spoken of 15 per cent of a certain amount which had to be expended in a certain time. I think that provision which may have been contained in other charters of. other railways, and provided for in the Railway Act, is made to prevent abuses by small companies, and people who might have charters which they wished to deal with, but not in the case of such a responsible company as the one we are dealing with. We know that it has the backing of the great institution to which I have just referred. That provision perhaps should only be invoked in the case of the Central Railway of. Canada or other railways which have existed only for a few years, where the people, who are at the head of them, are only after charters to try to bargain and make money with them. When we understand the reasons advanced in the Railway Committee on this occasion on behalf of the granting of this charter and also those propounded last week by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien), I do not see what reason this committee would have for refusing to grant an extension of this charter for two years more nor what harm there would be in granting that extension. We know this company intends to do this work when conditions improve somewhat. I am informed that

Esquimalt-Nanaimo Ry.
the construction of this part of the railway in that particular district of Vancouver Island forms part of a construction plan of a big organization; and while I do not know, it might be possible that it is not able, as my hon. friend has just pointed out, to commence immediately the construction of this part of the railway. When a company like that asks this Government and this House for an extension for two years and states that, within that period, it will probably be able to commence operations, I think we should believe the truth of its assertions and grant its request. Many members on both sides of the House, and especially on this side, are, I am sure, in favour of granting this request, and I think it would be a good move on the part of members of the Progressive party if they would support this bill and not support the amendment that the time for commencing operations be cut down to one year, as requested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I have not seen many such amendments agreed to in the last few years that I have been in the House. The Railway Committee has always taken into consideration the reasons advanced by these railway companies for renewals of their charters, and it has always granted what is fair and just. Therefore, I do not think we should make an exception in the case of this railway, but that we should give it the same terms as have been granted to many other railway companies.

I have been accused from time to time of speaking too fast. I have determined to cure myself of that fault. The subject before us to-night is one of the most momentous that might well engage our attention. It originates as you are aware, Mr. Chairman, with Bill No. 6. The official title of that bill is " Bill No. 6, An Act respecting The Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway Company." I see it is marked down here for its first reading on the 21st day of March, 1922, and that it has the signature of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie), who endorsed it, presumably, on its first introduction. The hon. member for Victoria, I might mention is not a resident of the district through which this railway runs, and therefore ii is natural to suppose that he is but im perfectly acquainted with the situation ol this railway in that district. It therefore becomes necessary for a humble representative of that district to go somewhat fully into the details of the situation. I address myself more particularly to the first clause (f the act, but in order that the committee
Esquimau-Nanaimo Ry.

may get a correct grasp of the situation, I will read the preamble as well.
Oh, oh.

I resent the levity with which some hon. gentlemen are treating this serious and important subject. As the thread of my argument has been somewhat disturbed by the interruptions, I had perhaps better begin again. The preamble reads as follows:
Whereas the Esquimau and Nanaimo Railway Company has by its petition prayed that it be enacted as hereinafter set forth, and it is expedient to grant the prayer of the said petition: Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:-
Then clause 1 of the bill follows:
The Esquimau and Nanaimo Railway Company, hereinafter called "the Company," may within two years after the passing of this act commence to construct the line of railway which it was authorized to construct by section two of chapter seventy-seven of the statutes of 1920, extending from a point at or near its present terminus at Courtenay, thence in a general easterly and northeasterly direction to a point at or near Duncan's Bay on the east coast of Vancouver Island, and may within five years after the passing of this act complete the said line of railway; and if within the said periods respectively, the said line is not commenced, or is not completed and put in operation, the powers of construction conferred upon the Company by Parliament shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said line as shall then remain uncompleted.
I wish to point out a decided discrepancy between the language used in this bill and in the original act to which it refers. You will observe that this bill says that starting from Courtenay the line will proceed "in a general easterly and north-easterly direction." If we refer to the act of 1920, which is chapter 77 of George V., second session of 1920-
Mr. McMASTER; Would the 'hon. member permit a question? Would the hon. member be able to speak a little louder so that we Would have the full benefit of his argument on this side of the House?
And of his wit.

I am perfectly willing to yield the point, but I wish to warn my hon. friend of this. In my younger and unregenerate days I once used to drive a team of oxen and any one who has had anything to do with driving oxen will agree with me that it can only be done by a man with a very loud voice and an absolute Command of profanity. I much fear that the forte of habit is so strong on me that if I do raise my voice to the pitch required to

make myself heard, I shall inevitably slip back into the old habit. If the hon. gentleman is ready to take that risk, I am quite willing to raise my voice. I understand that the hon. member imperfectly heard my opening remarks, so I am afraid I shall once more be compelled to go over the same ground again. Perhaps, however, it would be better to go through with the thread to begin with, and then I can rehearse my opening remarks afterwards, if I get through in time.
Section 2 of the act of 1920, which was assented to on the 11th of May of that year, provides that the company may construct and operate a line of railway from a point at or near its present terminus at Courtenay-the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is not paying attention to my remarks. Mr. Chairman, I am here to drive my points home if I have to repeat them a thousand times. You will observe that section 2 of the act of 1920 provides that this company,
-may lay out, construct, maintain and operate a line of railway from a point at or near its present terminus at Courtenay, thence in a general northerly and northeasterly direction-
You will notice that the original act says "in a general northerly and northeasterly direction," but the bill before us says "in a general easterly and northeasterly direction." Why, if this route is followed, the railway will have to be built in the gulf of Georgia, because that is the easterly direction from the point here named. We have seen many changes in the last three or four years, among them great political changes, but I do not think the direction of the cardinal points has shifted so much as is indicated In these two acts. I should like to know from the hon. member who is sponsor for this bill if he can tell me why the act in its original form describes the railway as running in a northerly direction, while the present bill has it going in an easterly direction. If the hon. member would like to make an explanation I am sure we would all be very happy to hear it.
Question.

I am sorry the hon. member will not oblige us on such a vital point. I know that a distinction of that kind is well calculated to sway the opinions of this House.
I think I have now indicated in a general way, Mr. Chairman, what is the purport of this bill. I think I should take a point of order on this subject, for the bill purports to be an amendment to this act;

Esquimalt-Nanaimo Ry.
but it is not in ordinary fact an amendment. It has been contended, I was informed the other day by one well in a position to know, that the original act with the powers contained in section 3 is still in existence, and that this bill is an amendment to it. But I would submit to hon. members who are lawyers that that is neither good law nor good parliamentary practice. This act will cease on the 11th day of May of this year, and I cannot see how this present bill can in any sense be considered-shall I say?-as concomitant or a part of it, unless it specifically says that section so-and-so shall be amended.
To illustrate the point I wish to make. If this amending bill purported to amend section 3 of the original act by striking out the date and putting in another date two years hence, that would be perfectly proper and correct and in accordance with parliamentary practice; but when it simply says, as it does here, that it has power to build the railway mentioned in section 2 of the original act, then I submit it cannot be held to be an amending bill, and consequently the original act will disappear on the 11th day of May, 1922. What then becomes of this section in the act dealing with the bonding privileges of the company? Section 4 of the act provides:
The securities issued by the company shall not exceed $50,000 per mile of the railway authorized by this act, and may be issued only in proportion to the length of railway constructed or under contract to be constructed.
Now, Sir, that section has disappeared in the so-called amending bill. Where then is the authority to be found to obtain money to build this railway? Is it not driven home to you, Mr. Chairman, and every member here that that has been omitted because the promoters know they will not need the money? In other words, they do not intend to build the railway, and they will be coming here two years, four years, ten years hence, and then it will be time enough to put in the bonding clauses. It has been contended, as I said, that the bonding clause in the original act governs this bill; but it cannot do so, for the reasons I have pointed out, that the act is not amended specifically, this bill only alludes to it in an indirect manner, so that-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is dealing now with the last amendment, whereas what he should discuss is the amendment after the word "railway" in line 17, as to the time for construction and completion of the railway.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I accept your direction, and I shall be very pleased to address myself more particularly to the amendment. In my haste to get the discussion over I was going on to the third amendment, but I will now devote myself more particularly to the amending of clause 1 by striking out all the words after "railway" in line 17. That, Sir, I am sorry to say, compels me to refer to section 3 of the Railway Act again, Chap. 68 of the Statutes of Canada of the year of Our Lord one thousand nine hundred and nineteen. Perhaps I ought to read the act from the beginning.
Yes.

Well, it is somewhat extended and I will not inflict it on hon. members. The heading of section 3 is " Construing of special acts." Subsection (a) reads as follows:
Except as in this act otherwise provided, (a; this act shall he construed as incorporate witl the special act.
I need not explain the meaning of that to hon. members. Subsection (b) provides:
Where the provisions of this act and of any special act passed by the Parliament of Canada relate to the same subject matter, the provisions of the special Act shall, in so far as is necessary to give effect to such special Act, be taken to override the provisions of this Act.
If hon. members do not understand that language it is not my fault; it is due to the peculiar legal phraseology employed. Put in plain English, it means that when a company comes to this House and brings a special railway act, it is supposed in its general lines to conform to the Railway Act of Canada, and what this special act does not specifically mention the general covers. But in this particular case they had inserted the words which I propose to strike out by that amendment. In that way the promoters are trying to take this bill out of the jurisdiction of the Railway Act, because the words that I propose to strike out read as follows:
-and if within the said periods respectively the said line is not commenced, or is not completed and put in operation, the powers of construction conferred upon the company by Parliament shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said line as shall then remain uncompleted.
To the ordinary layman, Mr. Chairman, those words would not appear to take this bill out of the jurisdiction of the Railway Act; but these provisions are always so astutely and so subtly phrased that they

Esquimau-Nanaimo Ry.
do not always mean what on the surface they appear to mean. I have my eye on it too, Mr. Chairman, and we will he a unit when it comes to nine o'clock! But, as I say, the insertion of these words, which to all appearances have nothing to do with the Railway Act, take the bill out of the jurisdiction of that act. Therefore I want to cut these words out, and then the bill would come under another section of the Railway Act, which I propose to read with your consent, Sir.
This is the same Railway Act that I alluded to before, Chap. 68 of the Statutes of Canada of the year of Our Lord one thousand nine hundred and nineteen, in two volumes-this is the first volume. Section 161 dealing with the powers of construction of railroads and the limitation of time for construction provides:
If the construction of the railway is not commenced and 15 per cent of the amount of the capital stock is not expended thereon in survey, purchase of right of way, and actual construction work, or in the case of a branch or extension of the railway, if 15 per cent of the bond issue authorized therefor is not expended thereon in actual construction work within two years after the passing of the act authorizing the construction of such railway, branch or extension, as the case may be, or where the Parliament of Canada grants an extension of time for commencing such contraction within the time so granted, or if the railway, or branch or extension, as the case may be, is not completed and put in operation within five years from the passing of such act, or where the Parliament of Canada grants an extension of time for completion within the time so granted, then the powers granted by such Act or by this Act shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the railway, or branch or extension, as the case may, as then remains uncompleted.
The common sense interpretation of that section is that the Railway Act of Canada specifies that a railway shall within two years commence construction and by construction is meant spending 15 per cent of the amount authorized of the bond issue for the building of that road or branch to be extended. Incidentally, I would like to ask, how does this railway company expect to arrive at this 15 per cent when they have not taken any authority to issue bonds? One can come to no other conclusion than that the bill is intended only as a stop-gap. My object in moving this amendment is to make the company come under the operation of the Railway Act of Canada, by striking out the words I have alluded to in clause 1 and putting nothing in their place. The company would then become obliged, under section 161, to spend 15 per cent of the capital cost of the railway in commencing operations 
within any period decided upon. So that while the House has decided, by the vote of the Chair-I should think the case almost unique in Canada-that this company shall have two years within which to commence operations, under the bill as introduced they have practically five years, because they do not really need to do anything definite in the way of commencing. A man can go out before breakfast with a shovel and do enough work to call it " commencing construction." I knew of a company which started construction in that way: they fulfilled the contract by stealing a couple of rails from a coal mine siding and laying them out along the route. Thar gave them three years more in which to carry on. It is to prevent something of that kind that my amendment is formulated. If this amendment passes, and the company, by the action of the committee tonight-I trust it may be only for to-night, for I presume there will be other opportunities of bringing the question up; as hon. gentlemen grow older, it is customary for them to grow wiser. We saw how the vote went last week; give us a little time and we will sweep this amendment through the House, probably by a unanimous vote. But I have got off the thread of my remarks.

I rise to a point of order. Rule 18, paragraph 2, provides that a member who talks for the purpose of gaining time may be ruled out of order. The hon. member clearly intimated his intention of talking the matter out until the clock should strike nine. Moreover, his arguments for the last ten minutes have been a tedious repetition, which brings them under the wording of Rule 18.
Mr. Chairman, I presume that is debatable.

Mr. Chairman, I thank you for your decision. While you may be a little shaky on an even vote, you are all right in your rulings. It is very embarrassing to be interrupted in this way by hon. members; it quite destroys the thread of my argument. I think I have made my case good; clearly it is desirable to pass this amendment so that my constituents will have at least the satisfaction of knowing that this company will pay out 15 per cent of the construction costs during the period decided upon. That is a substantial concession, but it is a reasonable one.

took recess at six o'clock I was about to ask the minister one question in regard to this item.
