Department of Trade and Commerce- Bounty on linen yarn spun in Canada from Canadian flax, including expenses of supervision ; under Orders-in-Council of September 3, 1918, and June 30, 1920, $26,000.
We would like to have a little information in regard to this item? Will the minister tell us exactly what this expenditure involves?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: This is the last year of these grants towards the cultivation of flax and the manufacture of linen yarns in Canada. The act under which assistance was granted was to run for three years, and this is the last year we make payments under the system adopted by the supervisors. The amount paid last year was about four thousand odd dollars but we have not received all the returns from the mills. We are asking for the same amount that was established last year.

I think this item should be held over until we get a little
1362	COMMONS
Supply-Trade and Commerce
more information. The details given to us by the minister are not very complete.

If my hon. friend desires any further information I am quite prepared to give it to him. He will notice there is no change in this vote. So far there is only one company receiving bounty, the Dominion Linens Limited of Guelph and the expenditure has been as follows: In 1920-21 on 139,796 pounds, bounty was paid of $5,096.11. The cost of supervision was $150.40. This bounty, as I have already told my hon. friend, was authorized under the War Measures Act to run for three years from April 1, 1919, and later was changed by Order-in-Council to run for three years from April 1st, 1920, so that it will expire in 1923.
Are we to understand that this is a re-appropriation?

The appropriation has to be voted each year, and in accordance with parliamentary procedure if the money is not earned within the year ending March 31st, it lapses and returns to the Treasury, but it must be voted each year.

Perhaps I can explain this item because I know something about it. It so happened that in the summer of 1918 it was impossible in Canada to get linen yarns. It was also impossible in Canada to get those classes of material into which linen yarns are manufactured. The question, I think, arose in the first instance through want of cloth for aeroplanes. An embargo was placed by Great Britain on Irish flax or linen yarns coming to this or any other country. The stock here had run out, also the stock in the United States. The threads that are used by shoemakers and harnessmakers was also exhausted, likewise fishing twines, and a serious question arose as to how these could be obtained; they were not manufactured in Canada at that time. The flax industry was being encouraged to some extent and there was a good deal of hope that it would develop into a large industry. The government of that day accordingly passed under the authority of the War Measures Act, an appropriation to the extent of $25,000 a year as a maximum to be paid in bounty on the production in Canada of linen yarns. No factory was ready to start that work, no factory in America was equipped for the purpose. A factory had been started in Philadelphia but 't had not been able to compete with the Irish, or Belgian linens, or with the linens from Japan. But the machinery was avail-

able there, and was subsequently purchased and brought to Canada. The bounty is paid at so much per pound.
Three cents.

With reference to linen yarn manufactured in Canada, only a small portion of the bounty has been earned. The factory in Guelph is the only one that has gone to the extent of actually manufacturing these linen yarns. I understand the amount earned last year was only five or six thousand dollars. It may be that that is not a full year's accounting, and that more will have to be paid, but the maximum as to amount was $25,000 per year, the limit of time was three years, and this is the last year.
May I ask the hon. gentleman, who seems to be acting as substitute for the Minister of Trade and Commerce, how much has been paid on account of this bounty?
Less than $10,000.

Perhaps the hon.
gentleman can give us some information as to the possibility of this becoming a paying industry in Canada or if the money is to be merely thrown away.

My hon. friend must remember that the bounty was given for the purpose of starting the industry. Our information is that this mill is running. The amount paid varies according to the quality of the thread. It provides for a bounty of 3 cents a pound to be paid on linen yarn not coarser than 12 lea, or finer than 20 lea, and 6 cents per pound for yarn 20 lea and finer but coarser than 40 lea, and 9 cents a pound for yarn 40 lea and finer. The amount appropriated under the original act was not to exceed $75,000 in all, and not to exceed $25,000 per year. My hon. friend will observe that, in placing this in the estimates, we are simply carrying out the Order in Council of 1920, and if the money is not earned there is nothing to pay.

I do not like to press it very much further, but, in view of the fact that this amount of money is not ordinarily required, I do not see the necessity for voting it. Could the hon. minister not cut it down to the actual amount required?

No, we cannot cut it down one cent, because Parliament three years ago advertised to industries that $25,000 a year was available for three years. You

Supply-Trade and Commerce
would not ask us to repudiate an act of Parliament. This is the last year. There is only one way of correcting it, and that is to repeal the act.

Item agreed to.
Dominion Bureau of Statistics (including census 1921), $415,000.
I think we should have from the minister some rather detailed statement as to how far advanced these statistics are, and when they will be ready for the country.

This information is handed out to the press, when completed. The information with respect to the provinces has been handed out, but we have not yet fully completed all the details for the different counties, cities, towns and townships. The staff is working at it continuously and we hope before long to be able to hand out a complete statement.
Will the minister tell us why, when the census was being taken, those who are born in Canada and have lived all their lives in Canada, cannot be registered as Canadians?

I have read that inquiry
frequently in the newspapers. My predecessor, was responsible for starting machinery to take the last census, and I imagine he followed the procedure of previous years, but I am forced to believe that the omission to which publicity was given in the last census will not occur again when we take the census of 1931.

Can the
minister not give us more information as to when the census is to be brought down? I am surprised to learn that the details are not ready. The final results are ready, and the final results, one would think could only be made up from the mass of details which the census department already has. What is the reason for the delay in knowing what the census is in the smaller group, when we have the information for the larger group ?

I think hon. gentlemen will
agree with me that there are volumes of figures to be compiled and checked, and, incidentally, I may take the House into my confidence, and say that we have dis^ covered some irregularities in the census. For instance, we discovered in some of the western towns that the census had been padded, and whole blocks had been put in which did not exist. Four enumerators
were brought before the court and fined. We had complaints from some of the eastern cities that there were omissions in the census. It is important that all these should be checked up carefully before the final report is handed out.
When do you expect it to be handed out?
I have urged the department to work as fast as possible and get it out.

The minister
has taken the House into his confidence, and I am going to be similarly frank with my hon. friend. Some people think the Government are not at all in a hurry to redistribute.

I heard that of the last
government.
It is thought to be a common fault with governments, and that the present Government are not at all anxious, at any rate, to provide for proper representation at the present minute.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Why not?

I leave that to my hon. friend to answer. I do not know why. Redistribution is very much overdue, and my hon. friend will tell us, of course, that we should have looked after it some months ago, although he says it cannot be looked after now. But a very easy way of preventing redistribution would simply be to delay bringing down the details of the census.

We have no desire to do
that.
I am delighted to receive that assurance. Can the minister tell us the cost of the census as against the other ordinary administration costs of the department?

I see, in the estimates for 1921-22, an item of $1,860,000 for expenses in connection with the taking of the census. This year, the amount is $415,000. Could the minister give us some idea as to the actual cost of taking the census of 1921?

That is a similar question to the one asked by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). Up to December 31, last, we had paid out on account of the Statistics Bureau including
1364	COMMONS
Supply-Trade and Commerce
census, $1,626,540.07. Of this amount, there was expended $97,194.58 for the bureau, and $1,529,345.49 for the census.

I did not receive from the minister any approximate date when he thought the census returns would be available for the House. The returns which, he understands, we are most anxious to have are, of course, those which would guide the House in the preparation of a redistribution bill. I think the House will agree that that is one of the most important things which we have ahead of us, and a matter which should not be delayed any longer than is absolutely necessary. The figures are all in the bureau at this time. The census was commenced last June, eleven months ago, and, under ordinary conditions, it should have been completed by this time-yes, before this time. The census returns are indispensable in the preparation of a proper redistribution bill, and until we get them, we cannot move in the matter. I was a little surprised, at an earlier date in the session, to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announce that the Government did not intend to proceed with redistribution at this session. I do not know that this affects Ontario so very much; from what I see in the newspapers, it may be that Ontario may lose one or two seats. That is not the point; the point is that the people are entitled to proper representation, no matter whether they live in Ontario or the West; and the minister, by putting on a few additional clerks, could bring down the necessary information to this House within a very few days. The question I asked the minister was: Are we to have this information or are we not? Those who live in parts of Canada where the representation is going to be very much affected, I should think, would join in the demand for early figures in regard to the census. I should be very glad if my hon. friend would give us to-night an approximate idea when he expects to lay before the House sufficient details of the census to enable the House to deal with a redistribution bill. The item which we are discussing now is the census item, and I think we should get that information before the item is passed.

I think I can go so far as to assure my hon. friend that, barring un-forseen events, the census will be completed and brought down in plenty of time to prepare a redistribution bill before there is a general election.

That is the purest kind of evasion. I think the minister must see that himself. There could not be a general election held in this country without a redistribution bill, unless we are going to administer a very severe wrench to our constitution. We must have the census figures. What is the reason for the delay? The statement of the minister tonight will not account for the delay. The employment of a few additional clerks would give us those figures next week, and I think, before the committee passes this item, it should get from the minister a definite promise that we are going to have those figures. It is all right to say that we shall have them before there is a general election. This Government is not in that altogether happy position that it can exactly say when we should or should not have a general election. All the more reason why we should have the census figures to enable us to have a proper redistribution bill.
To-morrow morning I will give instructions to the bureau to spur up a little, if it is possible to put on more help, and bring down the complete census.
Will the hon. gentleman say that the chief of the census staff is of opinion that they have not sufficient information now to warrant the introduction of a bill?
I did not say that.
Is he not the authority?
I did not say so.
I say he is.
Say what?
The Chief of the Statistics Branch. Will the hon. gentleman say that he is of opinion that the returns are not sufficient to warrant our going on with redistribution?

I have not offered any opinion in that regard. The question was asked when the census would be completed and brought down. I replied that some irregularities had been discovered in the census and that instructions had been issued not to give out complete returns to the printers, until the returns were all checked up and we could hand out a census that would be fairly satisfactory. The hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Meighen) w>as absent when I intimated to the House that we had discovered certain irregularities in western Canada; that four men had

Supply-Trade and Commerce
been fined for padding the lists, and that we have a grist of complaints from eastern Canada, from some cities, that names have been omitted. I am sure my hon. friends will agree with me that it is important that we should check up these returns and satisfy the people that the census handed out is a fair census. That work is being done as rapidly as possible. If my hon. friends desire that we should put on more help, I will ask the chief census enumerator to put on more help, if possible, and to spur up the work. We have no desire to delay completion of the census.

Small complaints as to persons being 'left out are one thing; I know nothing about that; but I saw some time ago census returns published as to several provinces, and I have read the address of the chief statistician. From that address no one could come to any conclusion save this, that the census is now and has been for some time quite sufficiently advanced for all the purposes of redistribution.

Is the right hon. gentleman aware of the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced to the House the other day that there would be no redistribution this year? I think the Prime Minister this year is master of the situation.
That may be a question. I was not discussing that. I was merely saying that, as regards the census returns, there is no excuse for lack of redistribution this session.

I think the minister should let this item stand over until he gives us some more definite information as to when those figures will 'be available, and fvhat is holding up the completion of the work. For the last two or three months, we have expected that those figures would be available. Some of my hon. friends around me seem to think this is not of a great deal of consequence for the province of Ontario. There is this to remark, that the part of Canada to which it is of real consequence, is apparently very quiescent and very acquiescent as regards the Government's action in not bringing down the figures. I should have thought, if people in any part of the Dominion of Canada showed urgency in regard to this matter, it would be hon. members from western provinces; and if they are prepared to acquiesce in the delay and to postpone any possibility of redistribution this session, I do not know that people from Ontario are
so very much concerned about the matter. But the wonderful silence on the part of all hon. members from Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba in regard to this question is certainly most impressive.

It is encouraging, almost inspiring indeed, to learn that my hon. friends to my right have become converted to the necessity for redistribution. I want to say that silence is no indication of acquiescence. There is on the Order Paper to-day, I understand, a resolution by a member of this group calling the attention of this House to the desirability of enacting a measure of redistribution this session, if possible. I want to associate myself very heartily with the earlier statement made by my hon. friend from South Wellington, that it is very desirable we should have the actual facts concerning the recent census at the earliest possible date with the object of passing a redistribution bill.

I would also like to point out a reason for urgency in this matter. I come from the county of York, a riding that is partly urban and partly rural. In the last election the total number of voters on the list of South York was 49,700. That constituency is entitled to at least three seats. While the city of Toronto and the county of York have ten members in this House, they are really entitled according to population, so far as we know the figures, to twenty members. We ought to have twenty. It is now proposed to introduce the principle of proportional representation in electing representatives to this House. The city of Toronto would like to know how long it is going to be without a fair representation in this House, and whether the principle of proportional representation is to govern at the next election. If so, it will effect an absolute revolution in the city of Toronto and the county of York, and that being the case, we are entitled to know the actual census figures at the earliest possible moment. I believe the figures could be easily prepared and given to the public; I do not think it is necessary to take so much time over it. We cannot have the information too soon, especially in view of so much talk about another election being held any day in this country. We want to have these figures so that we can study them and devise some means of bringing about an equality between the representation of the cities and of the rural portions. While Ontario would not have any more seats, surely the cities by reason of their growth in population are

Supply-Trade and Commerce
entitled to greater representation than they now have. As a matter of fact, the city of Toronto and the county of York include about one-fourth of the population of Ontario, and if one man's vote is as good as another man's, we ought to have one-fourth of Ontario's representation in this House, whereas we have a good deal less than one-eighth.

With reference to the
Bureau of Statistics, I should like to ask the minister what progress has been made in unifying the work of gathering statistics for all departments of the Government. At present, if one wants statistics dealing with a certain branch of the Government, it is sometimes very difficult to get them without hunting up a certain branch, or a certain section of that branch, or a certain department, or something of that sort, and being referred from one to the other. On one occasion last year I was referred from one branch to another seven or eight times before I succeeded in getting certain figures I required in regard to minerals. That is very annoying. There should he one central place where we could get statistics relating to any department and any branch of the Government, and I should like to know what advancement has been made in the working out of such a central system.

That work is being gradually co-ordinated. I myself have had occasion to find fault with the duplication of information that is asked for throughout the country. In so far as it is possible, this duplication is being eliminated and the work centralized in the bureau of which Mr. Coats has charge.
The object ultimately is that Mr. Coats' office will be able to give statistics relating to any branch of the government?
Yes.
What is there, if anything, that is not in the statistics office now?
The Department of Labour have a statistical branch, as well as the Mines Department and the Department of the Interior.

There is no statistical branch in the Department of the Interior. There is a Natural Resources branch, which gathers information of course, but that is not statistics, and such figures as it does gather go immediately to the statis-

tics office. If there is a branch gathering statistics in the Department of Labour, it would occur to me there is no need of it, as the work should all be done in the Statistics branch.

Perhaps my hon. friend is right. I know that the figures that are gathered in the Interior Department are sent to Mr. Coats' office. I remember some months ago a man wanted to be transferred from that work in the Interior Department to Mr. Coats' branch.
I know that every requisition of the hon. gentleman's department to the Interior with regard to the transfer of statistics was met by the Interior Department. There was no reservation.
How many enumerators were employed on the last census, and what proportion of them were soldiers?
There were 11,414 enumerators. We have no record as to the number of returned soldiers employed, but a number of returned soldiers were engaged on this work.
In my riding in every case where the work of taking the census could be given to returned jnen, that was done. The majority of the work was done by returned men and done fairly well.

The British North America Act has very wisely provided that the representation of this House should be based on the representation of the province of Quebec. As a commissioner of the city of Montreal for some years, I am familiar with conditions existing in that city, and I cannot approve too strongly the stand taken by the minister to make doubly certain that the census figures, for the island of Montreal more especially, are authentic and accurate. It is a well known fact to those who read the Montreal papers that when the preliminary census figures were given out, several newspapers in Montreal, La Presse, La Patrie, the Montreal Star, as well as the Chambre de Commerce and others, protested against the figures and alleged 1hat the census that had been taken within the city limits was inaccurate and incomplete. Petitions were signed and circulated calling on the Government to verify the figures, so I hope the minister before a final announcement is made, if he has not already taken the necessary steps to verify

Supply-Trade and Commerce
these charges, will do so, so that when we get the census report for the province of Quebec and of the island of Montreal we shall know that it is absolutely accurate and complete. The figures for the city of Montreal, properly speaking, are misleading because they only give the population within che municipal limits. The outlying towns, Westmount, Outremont, and so on, are left out of the complete figures for Montreal as they are generally given.
Generally speaking, I think it is the duty of the minister and of the Government to make doubly sure that these charges have been fully investigated so that the figures finally given out may be absolutely satisfactory. This is a matter in which not only the province of Quebec, but every province in the Dominion is interested. If the members from Ontario and the West are anxious to have a change in the representation of this House, they must be certain that the basis on which the work is done is absolutely accurate, and that the figures that are finally given are the correct figures which the country should have.

Is it not a fact that
the checking up has all been done as respects Montreal? There is no doubt now as to the figures?

The checking up as respects Montreal has been fairly well completed. It is only right to say that in many cases we discovered the complaints were scarcely justified. There were many irregularities, but they were not of as grave a character as was at first thought and reported through the press. For the further information of my hon. friend, I have here the last report of the Commissioner of the Census up to the 20th of April. He intimates that the returns were being handed out as finally revised, but that in the case of the province of Quebe- there was more than the ordinary amount of revision found necessary, and he would like to spend a few days longer on the final revision. I imagine the returns will be completed in a very few days.
Does he indicate how much revision still remains to be done?
No.

On the 20th
of April he intimated that the final work would be done in a very few days. That is twelve days ago. Does not the minister think this vote might well stand over until he has those final returns?

If my hon. friend insists
upon it I do not object, but I can assure him that we will speed up the work tomorrow. We are just as anxious as he is to have it completed.
Have all the enumerators and other census officers been paid in full?

So far as I know all those
whose reports have been passed upon and approved have been paid; but only a few days ago some cases were brought to my attention where enumerators-one in the eastern part of Quebec-had failed to send in final returns. Until we get those final returns we are not going to make payment. In those cases we have had to send men especially down to look into the returns.

I feel that I shouldalthough I do not hope to change any opinion as a result-say a few words with regard to a remark that fell from the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), as regards those on this side of the House only lately favouring redistribution. The fact is, as was stated in the House last session-although I do not suppose the statement got very wide circulation where such circulation was not profitable-that I made every attempt to have the census so advanced that we could introduce a redistribution bill last session. I conferred with the Chief of the Statistics Branch, who informed me that owing to a change in the law made about ten years ago the census was taken on the first of June instead of three months earlier, as had previously been the case. I canvassed with him the possibility of advancing the date again to the first of March and rushing the census so that redistribution could be introduced during the session. Upon investigation the Chief of the Statistics branch reported to me that it would be impossible so to do, that even by advancing the census three months not more than one month at the very outside would be gained, owing to the difficulty of getting work done at that unfavourable period of the year, the roads and weather conditions being what they would be, and that consequently it would not be possible to be through with the work earlier than September; but that taking the census at the time fixed by law, namely, the first of June, it would in his judgment be possible to have the return ready in October. I had a letter from him to that effect.
Esquimalt-Nanaimo Ry.

During a discussion last session I stated that in my judgment we would not be justified in dissolving Parliament at that time in response to demands from hon. gentlemen, then in the opposition. One reason I gave was that it was very important to have redistribution before dissolution, and I stated that I was most anxious to have it.
It developed in the fall, at a further conference with the Chief Statistician of the Census branch, that it would be the month of December before the census returns were ready, such had been the slow progress made as a result of many unforeseen difficulties that had been encountered, and that there would be no possibility of securing census returns sufficient to warrant going on with a redistribui tion bill until at least the month of December, that that month would be late enough and by that time the census returns would be available. That meant redistribution could not be put through at any special session, and that if it was to be attended to before dissolution we would have to have a regular session. Under the circumstances I feel that a regular session would not be justified even for the purpose of redistribution. Those are the facts.
It now transpires that it would not have been possible even in December. I feared that might be the case, because I knew that already completion of the census returns was two months beyond the time that had been fixed first in the spring, and if that should be the case we would be in a very unfortunate position indeed. Consequently I felt it my duty not to wait for redistribution. But for hon. gentlemen to try to lead the House to believe that there was any aversion on my part to redistribution, or that the importance of it was not appreciated, is entirely to mislead the House, although not done intentionally.
Now, I do think that we undoubtedly have information enough-I cannot think it can be otherwise having read the addresses and the information given by the Chief Statistician-I say that we undoubtedly have information enough to warrant the introduction of a redistribution bill at the earliest possible date.
This session?
At this session.

Is it the intention to gradually include all statistical clerks from the various departments of the Government under this one head, because I notice on page 104 under the details of civil govern-

ment that there are 91 statistical clerks employed at a salary of $85,055? Is that in addition to the amount of half a million dollars under this head?
Page 104 refers to civil employees.

But are the salaries included in this Dominion Bureau under this
item?

No, that money represents the salaries that we have voted under civil
government estimates.

But this item we have
now, No. 360?

No, this is for the salaries of enumerators and others who took the
census.

Is it not a fact that these census enumerators were appointed by the Government without the assistance of the Civil Service Commission, and that in these appointments we have had patronage exercised in its most evil form?

I do not hear any
answer. An answer might possibly embarrass the Gove* .iment, if it ever hopes to be in office for another census. I would suggest to the hon. member that he inquire as to the possibility of appointments under the Civil Service Commission for temporary work of this nature, requiring very often re-appointment to the same office for a very few days in succession. The hon. member knows that as well as anyone else. All I hope for from this Government is that they maintain the Civil Service Act in the form in which it is to-day-indeed, that is somewhat beyond my hopes. If they succeed in doing that, then there will at least be less cause for complaint than there has been in the past. If, however, the hon. member feels like introducing a motion now, as a government supporter, for the appointment under the Civil Service Commission of officials doing enumerating temporarily once in ten years, it will be an evidence of loyalty to that act that I do not expect from hon. gentlemen opposite.
What I complain about particularly is that of the thousands who were appointed everyone seems to have been a supporter of the past government.

The minister has said that the delay was caused through one or two of the eastern constituencies not being yet fully reported. In

Supply-Trade and Commerce
my own constituency some of the enumerators complain that they are still unpaid. Of course, these men were not appointed by me; I was not even consulted. But they are complaining to this day, and I would like to know how the matter stands.

It is exactly in my hon. friend's consituency that the trouble arises. The Chief Commissioner in Bonaventure has been dilatory in sending in returns, particularly those relating to the accounts of the persons who worked under him. It was necessary to send a man down there.

Before the resolution carries it seems to me that we ought to have something definite from the ministerial benches as to the attitude they take. Does redistrubtion depend, in the opinion of the minister, upon the completion of that part of the work which has not yet been reported? Or does the mihistelr agree with the leader of the Opposition when he says that there is already enough information available on which to base a redistribution bill? If we are to be told that because of a little trouble in this or that constituency there is to be no redistribution, we want to know it now. On the other hand, if the attitude of the Government is that the census enumeration has advanced to such a point that there is no reason why a redistribution bill should not now be brought down-very good; I have no objection to the item passing. But if that information is not forthcoming, then this item should be held up until we find out exactly what position the work is in; and this is the only opportunity of ascertaining that.

May I remind my hon friend, in the first place, of the statement of the leader of the Opposition that it is very hard to determine exactly when this work will be completed? The leader of the Opposition has just told us that in the case of the last census he was disappointed on three different occasions and found its completion delayed. In 1911 we took a census in this country, and we did not have a redistribution bill until the session of 1914.
Did the hon. gentleman say 1914?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No; I have a clear recollection that the redistribution bill was passed in June, 1914.

The act is chapter 61 of the statutes of 1914; it was assented to in June, 1914. I had the honour of being on that committee. The committee was appointed immediately after the House assembled in January, and its labours were not completed until June. To readjust the boundaries of constituencies all over the Dominion where county boundaries do not exist and where the population has increased in urban centres; to provide for the fair adjustment of boundaries in the cities, is no easy task. Hon. gentlemen who have had to do with work of this kind will realize that a redistribution, in order to be successful, would occupy the attention of Parliament for three or four months.

That is all the more reason why we should not further delay this matter; we should get at it at the earliest possible moment. Now, there was this difference between the situation in 1911 and that in 1922. In 1911 the Conservative party had a large majority in the House; there was no chance in those days of anything giving way. But that is not the case with this Government; from what we have seen during this session there are all kinds of chances in the present circumstances. But the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made up his mind-I have no doubt that he has his leader's authority for it-that there will be no redistribution bill this session and that, therefore, there is no need for
10 p.m. haste; he can jog along with these figures and bring them down at the end of the session or the beginning of next session. He can see, if he opens his eyes, that there is no very serious demand from the Progressive party for a redistribution bill this session-that is, if we may judge from their attitude in the House to-night.

I do not know what the figures are, and I am not saying they were not delayed in the past. But I do think the committee has a right to know now exactly how this matter stands; we should not be put off with vague statements as to troubles here or troubles there. We want to know whether there is enough information in the hands of the Government to enable the House to consider this question. It is an easy thing for the minister to get that information, and I am afraid he will have to get it.

I will be prepared to give my hon. friend such information as I have,



Supply-Trade and Commerce
but I will rot guarantee the figures are eom_ plete. As the leader of the Opposition said a few moments ago, this matter is entirely in the hands of the Chief Statistician. Surely my hon. friend does not ask me to hand out reports the correctness of which he himself cannot be assured.

I am not asking that at all. But the minister only a moment ago mentioned correspondence he had received from the census commissioner, indicating that the reports might be finished in a few days. All I ask is that we have the information down to date.
As soon as it is finished, I will give it to my hon. friend.
No; I want the hon. gentleman to find out now how it stands and when the final report can be made.

Before the resolution is declared carried I want to refer briefly to the remarks made by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). I think his remarks were entirely out of place. I am a new member in this House and know very little of the mode of procedure, but it seemed to me that the hon. member was a little out of order: I understood we were passing estimates and not discussing the matter of redistribution. For my part, I feel that we should have redistribution and that we should have it at this session. I understand that an opportunity will be afforded later to discuss that matter and if there is, I will place myself on record then. But I cannot allow the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for South Wellington to pass without letting him know where I stand.

My hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Coote) says that he is a new member, and that explains why he would give any great attention to the remarks of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). Now if we are to take the opinion of the leader of the Opposition seriously we would not be losing all this time on the present item because he told the committee that we had enough information, or at any rate that the minister would have enough, to justify proceeding with the redistribution bill. As my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) said, we are discussing this estimate and not the subject of redistribution. Therefore I would say to tMr. Robb.]
you Mr. Chairman, that we had better deal with the present item and not venture upon a discussion of redistribution at the present time. When we come to the matter of redistribution the curiosity of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), I am sure, will be set at rest, to our satisfaction at any rate. In connection with this matter I am sure the minister has every right to take the stand that he has taken. As has been pointed out my hon. friends to the right appointed these officials. The present minister did not have anything to do with the matter and had no chance to appoint competent officials; consequently he has had to put up with the work of men appointed by the late government. The work, in many districts, has been poorly done- that is evident-and we will have to wait until we get satisfactory information. This the minister has promised in good time.

When we listen so often to hon. members to our left calling us down for delaying the business of the House it makes us feel a little bit fatigued to say the least. To-night we had to sit here for one whole hour listening to the tiresome repetition of arguments intended to kill a certain bill.
Order.
My hon. friend does not want to make a misstatement. The hon. member who occupies the floor in reference to the bill referred to is not connected with the Progressive party.
I am quite agreeable that my hon. friend should disown-
And he was not out of order, Mr. Chairman.

My hon. friend from
Comox-Alberni, (Mr. Neill) knows something about being out of order because he was out of order for a solid hour this evening. I was remarking for my hon. friend (Mr. Johnston) that although he might not claim the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, at the same time hon. members to my left voted solidly in favour of killing the bill in question. Therefore, when we are looking for a little information on a subject like this it is not open to my hon. friend from Last Mountain to address lectures to us in view of such actions on the part of hon. members sitting around him.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

None of us who sat in the House with the hon. member for Last Mountain and witnessed his unfailing fidelity to the Liberal party, irrespective wholly of where he sits, are surprised now when, in any difficulty, we see him coming through the fog and the mist with the lifeboat to whatever minister may be in trouble. If the minister will say that the expression of belief that I gave is right-that in so far as the census returns are concerned there is no reason on that score for the delay of redistribution-then the subject of redistribution enters no further into the discussion on this item. This item bears on redistribution only to the extent that it involves the question as to whether we are far enough on now to go ahead or not. Now, I took the responsibility of expressing the opinion-from what I had read, from what I had seen issued from the census office-that we are. If the minister will say that is right then, so far as I am concerned, there is no objection at all to the item passing; but I would not like to have the item pass without any information as to the extent the census has advanced and then, when the resolution of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Shaw) comes up, have it met by hon. gentlemen opposite with the assertion " Oh we are not far enough on with the census." Let us know before this item passes if we are far enough on so far as the census is concerned. Then, well and good-there ends the relationship of redistribution to this item.

As the data for any particular group of census districts, cities, towns, etc., became available they have been given to the press, during the past fall and winter, in the form of mimeographed sheets for simultaneous publication. In each case the figures were given as preliminary only. In this way, the results for the several provinces, by electoral districts, and for the leading cities and towns of Canada, [DOT]were given out between September 1921 and March 1922. Altogether nineteen statements of this kind were issued.
As the returns for each province become available in finally revised form they are being issued in printed leaflets. Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have already appeared in this form, and similar bulletins for Manitoba, and British Columbia are in the press. Those for Saskatchewan and Ontario will follow next week-

I do not dispute the accuracy of the statement but it does not say whether or not the census is far enough advanced. If that is all the information the minister has, and he does not know whether or not the census is far enough advanced, there is no reason why he should not know by Thursday-no reason at all. He can go to his chief statistician and come to this House and say "yes" or "no" in reply to the question. Now would it not be well to have that information definitely before we go further?

The estimates of the Trade and Commerce Department will not all be passed to-night and when the estimates of the department are up again I may have that information for him. But my right hon. friend was Prime Minister. He himself thought at one time to have a revision. He was disappointed and he fixed another date. Again he was disappointed and another date was fixed on. For the third time he was disappointed.
Just twice.
I will give my hon. friend a promise to bring down the information when we go into committee again. In the meantime I suggest we make some progress.

Before
leaving this subject I call attention to this one fact: Before the last census was undertaken the then Minister of Trade and Commerce through the chief statistician wrote to every member of the House to ascertain whether he had recommendations to make as to the manner in which the census should be taken in his constituency. I made certain recommendations for my constituency, and inquired whether I would have anything to say as to the appointment of the census officers and enumerators. I was told "No", and the result of it is that not being consulted I did not nominate anybody. To this day a number of these men remain

unpaid, and the department has to send men down to the constituency in order to clear up the situation. Now I believe in the popular representatives having something to say with respect to these matters, particularly as regards their own constituencies. If I had been consulted as regards the county of Bonaventure, bearing in mind the experience that I have had on two other occasions, I certainly would have given advice that would have saved all this trouble, and the same remark applies to many other members. The hon. member reminds the committee of some trouble in the past in the county of Bonaventure. The minister has stated that formerly this printing was done in various departments. Will he tell us if he has effected economies by consolidating the printing under one department?
That was the idea of the consolidation. We shall be able to measure that when the returns are all completed.

In the absence of a little defence for the previous government by the minister, I cannot allow my hon. friend (Mr. Johnson), with his usual subtlety, to get away with the suggestion carefully concealed or partially veiled in his question. I have another question to ask in connection with this item, and I should like to assure the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) that he gave me credit for something that was not in my mind. I had rather thought this estimate of more importance than the reputation of any party. The question I would like to ask is: To what extent is there a demand for these government publications? I speak from observation covering a number of years, and it seems to me that, in past years, no matter what party happened to be in power, some sections of the country were flooded at times with publications that were not needed. I believe they have a value; but they have a value only if they go into the hands of those who will read them. Are they asked for, or does the department distribute them more or less indiscriminately ?

They a're asked for, and the mailing list is revised periodically. Post cards are sent out asking those who have received these reports if they desire them continued. If no reply comes, the names of those who do not reply are eventually
CMr. Robb.]
taken off the list, and the list is revised from time to time.

The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Johnson), has brought up a question of some importance. I suppose, as a member of Parliament, a man receives a fairly liberal supply of these publications. I think I can speak for the average member of this House when I say that fully one-half of the publications, which are issued by the government and sent to the individual member, are of no practical use at all. We do not look at them; we do not open them; we consign them to the waste-paper basket a minute or two after we receive them. I am sorry to say that my experience has been that many business houses which receive these reports do the same thing. The mailing list could be very greatly curtailed. Five or six years ago the quantity of unnecessary printing that was done in this country was a positive scandal, and we undertook to see what could be done to remedy that difficulty. Not only was the number of publications greatly reduced, but the mailing list was greatly reduced. I believe the minister would perform a very valuable service if he would look into the question of a further reduction of the mailing-list and also a further reduction in the number of publications. In my own case, and I think it is the case with every member of this House and every member of the local legislatures in this Dominion, more than half what is sent might well be dispensed with and that money saved. If the minister will give that matter his consideration I think he will do a valuable service.
I will give my hon. friend that assurance so far as my own department is concerned. I cannot be responsible for other departments.
